planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once soil has warmed; growth is extremely slow in the first few years.

directions: This unusual date palm from the Himalayan foothills never forms a visible trunk, instead sending up a tight rosette of stiff, spine-tipped fronds directly from ground level. Give it gritty, sharply drained soil and keep young plants in light shade, moving them into fuller sun as they mature and thicken. It shrugs off summer drought and brief winter cold once established, but resents sitting in wet soil through the dormant season. Use it as a low, textural accent in a dry rock garden or gravel bed rather than as a shade or screening plant.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant out after all frost danger has passed; protect trunks the first couple of winters in zone 9b.

directions: A small Brazilian feather palm prized for its finely segmented, slightly twisted leaflets and compact single trunk, making it a good fit for courtyards and tight entryway beds where a queen palm would be too large. Plant it in well-drained soil in an open, sunny spot and water regularly through hot weather, letting the soil dry somewhat between waterings. Growth is very slow, so expect a modest, slowly thickening specimen rather than a quick screen. It tolerates brief dips into the upper 20s F but should be sited with some winter wind protection at the northern edge of its range.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into lean, open ground; seed can take a year or more to sprout.

directions: Native to the open grassland campos of central Brazil, this is the smallest member of the Butia clan, staying nearly trunkless and hugging the ground like a coarse ornamental grass in its first years. Give it full sun and lean, fast-draining soil, since it naturally grows in competition with grasses on thin, nutrient-poor ground and resents rich, soggy beds. In cultivation, away from grass competition and with occasional light feeding, it fills out noticeably larger than wild specimens while keeping its distinctive silvery, densely woolly flower spathes. Treat it as a slow, long-lived rock-garden or xeriscape accent rather than a fast landscape filler.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Set divisions or containers out in spring in shaded beds; clumps thicken very slowly.

directions: A little-grown understory relative of lady palm from southern China and Vietnam, distinguished by noticeably thinner canes and sparser, narrower leaf segments than the common Rhapis excelsa. It wants the same shaded, humus-rich, evenly moist conditions as its relatives and resents hot afternoon sun or soil that dries out completely. Clumps are strikingly slow to bulk up, even slower than Rhapis multifida, so patience is needed before it forms a dense thicket of canes. Use it in a shaded courtyard or understory planting where its delicate, fine-textured foliage can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant into consistently wet, boggy ground once nighttime lows are reliably warm; this is a true wetland palm.

directions: Unlike its desert-adapted relatives, this clustering date palm comes from brackish mangrove swamps of South and Southeast Asia and actually thrives with its roots in permanently soggy, even periodically flooded, ground. Site it at a pond edge or low rain-garden basin where other date palms would rot, and give it the dappled light of a woodland or wetland margin rather than blasting full sun. Multiple slender, spine-armed stems rise from a clustering base, eventually forming a dense multi-trunked thicket useful for screening a water feature. It has essentially no frost tolerance, so it is only reliable in the warmest, most tropical pockets of the Gulf Coast.
